title: Babies followed a gaze plus a point more than a gaze alone
summary: In that same monthly study, infants followed a combined gaze-and-point cue more often than gaze alone.
body: Tang, Gonzalez, and Deak compared three cues: gaze direction, a pointing gesture, and both together. The infants followed the combination more than gaze by itself. Pointing alone sat in between and was not reliably different from the other cues. The design used reward videos so the motive to look would be similar across ages. The result is about cue strength in this lab, not about which gesture a child uses at home. The sample is the same 43 infants plus a smaller comparison group. Paraphrased from a CC BY-NC-ND article.

sources.title: The slow emergence of gaze- and point-following
sources.author: Yueyan Tang, Marybel Robledo Gonzalez, and Gedeon O. Deak
sources.note: Supports greater following of combined gaze-and-point cues than gaze alone, with points intermediate. Paraphrase only (CC BY-NC-ND).
